title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
This week

define our own types: records and unions
let the compiler check every case
count a type’s values, and spot impossible states
option: the honest answer to “there might be nothing”


Two ways of building types, and you can describe almost any data precisely.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Problem: a cash register
A register knows each article’s code, name, and price.
A purchase is a list of items: a number of pieces and an article code.
Make the bill: for each item, pieces, name, and line total; plus the grand total.

Your turn. With lists and tuples from Week 3: what types would you use?

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Hansen’s model: tuples with names
type ArticleCode = string
type ArticleName = string
type Price = int
type Register = (ArticleCode * (ArticleName * Price)) list
type NoPieces = int
type Item = NoPieces * ArticleCode
type Purchase = Item list
type Info = NoPieces * ArticleName * Price
type Bill = Info list * Price

type Price = int is only a second name for int: an abbreviation, not a new type.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
The bill, with tuples
let rec findArticle code register =
    match register with
    | [] -> failwith ("unknown article code " + code)
    | (c, article) :: _ when c = code -> article
    | _ :: rest -> findArticle code rest

let rec makeBill register purchase =
    match purchase with
    | [] -> ([], 0)
    | (pieces, code) :: rest ->
        let (name, price) = findArticle code register
        let lineTotal = pieces * price
        let (lines, total) = makeBill register rest
        ((pieces, name, lineTotal) :: lines, lineTotal + total)

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Which int is which?
val makeBill:
  register: (string * ('a * int)) list ->
    purchase: (int * string) list -> (int * 'a * int) list * int

Your turn. In (int * 'a * int) list * int, what does each int mean?


You can only tell by position. Swap two ints by mistake: it still compiles.


We need a way to name the parts.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option

A tuple with named parts
type Article = { Name: string; Price: int }

let coffee = { Name = "iced coffee"; Price = 45 }
let price = coffee.Price                        // 45


type Article = { … } defines a new type
{ Name = …; Price = … } creates one; F# finds the type from the field names
coffee.Price reads a field

Predict: “changing” a record
let promo = { coffee with Price = 40 }   // a NEW record
After this, what is coffee.Price?

Still 45. { coffee with Price = 40 } is a new record: immutable, as always.

let describe { Name = name; Price = price } =
    $"{name}: {price} baht"

let same = coffee = { Name = "iced coffee"; Price = 45 }   // true


Compared by content, like tuples. (Not true for ordinary objects in Java or C#.)

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Problem: shapes
A shape is either a circle, a rectangle, or a triangle.

Your turn. Can you model this with records and tuples? What goes wrong?

Students usually propose a record with a “kind” string and fields for every shape. Ask: what is the radius of a rectangle?

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
A union type
type Shape =
    | Circle of radius: float
    | Rectangle of width: float * height: float
    | Triangle of a: float * b: float * c: float

let wheel = Circle 0.3
let door = Rectangle (0.9, 2.0)
let sail = Triangle (3.0, 4.0, 5.0)


One of the cases, each with its own data. All three are Shapes.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
section: Problem: the area of a shape
text:
Problem: the area of a shape
area (Rectangle (0.9, 2.0)) = 1.8

Before the code: how many rules will the match have? What does each one bind?

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
area: one rule per case
let area shape =
    match shape with
    | Circle r -> System.Math.PI * r * r
    | Rectangle (w, h) -> w * h
    | Triangle (a, b, c) ->
        let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0                // Heron's formula
        sqrt (s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c))

Constructors are patterns: Rectangle (w, h) matches only rectangles, and binds the data.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Forget a case
> let area shape =
      match shape with
      | Circle r -> System.Math.PI * r * r;;

warning FS0025: Incomplete pattern matches on this expression.
For example, the value 'Rectangle (_, _)' may indicate a case
not covered by the pattern(s).

Add | Ellipse of … to Shape next year: every match in the program that misses it gets a warning.


In this course: every FS0025 is a bug.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Predict: month 13
Week 1’s daysInMonth 2025 13 returned 0. Now:
type Month =
    | January | February | March | April | May | June
    | July | August | September | October | November | December
Your turn. How do you write “month 13” now?

You can’t. The problem isn’t handled; it’s removed.
let isLeapYear year =
    (year % 4 = 0 && year % 100 <> 0) || year % 400 = 0

let daysIn year month =
    match month with
    | February -> if isLeapYear year then 29 else 28
    | April | June | September | November -> 30
    | _ -> 31

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Each case, its own data
type Payment =
    | Cash of received: int
    | Card of lastFour: string
    | PromptPay of phone: string

let receiptLine total payment =
    match payment with
    | Cash received -> $"Cash {received}, change {received - total}"
    | Card lastFour -> $"Card ending {lastFour}"
    | PromptPay phone -> $"PromptPay to {phone}"

Compare: one record with fields for cash, card, and phone, most of them meaningless.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Counting values

|\texttt{bool}| = 2, \ |\texttt{unit}| = 1, \ |\texttt{Month}| = 12


Tuples and records multiply (“AND”):
|A \mathbin{*} B| = |A| \times |B| \qquad |\texttt{bool * Month}| = 24


Unions add (“OR”):
|\;\texttt{C1 of A | C2 of B}\;| = |A| + |B|


Products and sums: algebraic data types.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Problem: a traffic light
// red, amber, green: each lamp on or off
type LampsOn = bool * bool * bool

Your turn. How many values does LampsOn have? How many are real?


2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8 values; only 3 are real. Every function must decide what “red and green” means.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Make illegal states unrepresentable
type Light =
    | Red
    | Amber
    | Green

let next light =
    match light with
    | Red -> Green
    | Green -> Amber
    | Amber -> Red

Exactly 3 values, all real. next has nothing to check.


Count the values; compare with reality. Week 9 builds a whole design method on this.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Problem: no answer
What should each of these return?

maximum []
lookup "juice" prices, when there’s no juice
month number 13


So far: failwith (crash), or a magic value like 0 or -1.


Your turn. What’s wrong with the magic value?

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
option: just a union
type 'a option =
    | None
    | Some of 'a

let some3 = Some 3                     // int option
let nothing : int option = None


|\texttt{'a option}| = |\texttt{'a}| + 1: every value, plus “nothing”.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Functions that might not answer
let rec tryLookup key table =
    match table with
    | [] -> None
    | (k, v) :: _ when k = key -> Some v
    | _ :: rest -> tryLookup key rest
val tryLookup:
  key: 'a -> table: ('a * 'b) list -> 'b option when 'a: equality

The type says it honestly: you might not get a 'b. By convention: try in the name.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
You can’t forget to check
> let x : int = Some 3;;
error FS0001: This expression was expected to have type 'int'
but here has type ''a option'

let priceText item table =
    match tryLookup item table with
    | Some price -> $"{item}: {price} baht"
    | None -> $"{item}: not on the menu"


Forget None, and: FS0025 … the value 'None' may indicate a case not covered.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
The antidote to null
null / None / undefined hides inside any variable. Forget to check: NullPointerException, Cannot read properties of undefined. Tony Hoare: his “billion-dollar mistake”.


Absence is in the type. A string is always a string; only a string option might be missing.
You can’t forget to check. No int out of an int option without handling None.
Check once, at the boundary. After the match, the value is plain.



The habit: might have no answer? Return an option. Never a magic value.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Options at the boundaries
let monthFromNumber n =
    match n with
    | 1 -> Some January | 2 -> Some February | 3 -> Some March
    | 4 -> Some April | 5 -> Some May | 6 -> Some June
    | 7 -> Some July | 8 -> Some August | 9 -> Some September
    | 10 -> Some October | 11 -> Some November | 12 -> Some December
    | _ -> None

A number from outside can be invalid: option. A Month inside your program is always valid.

The register, without crashing
let rec tryFindArticle code register =
    match register with
    | [] -> None
    | (c, article) :: _ when c = code -> Some article
    | _ :: rest -> tryFindArticle code rest

Problem: a list type from scratch
Every list is [], or x :: rest.

Your turn. Write that as a union type.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
MyList
type MyList<'a> =
    | Empty
    | Cons of 'a * MyList<'a>

let rec myLength xs =
    match xs with
    | Empty -> 0
    | Cons (_, rest) -> 1 + myLength rest

Empty is []; Cons (x, rest) is x :: rest. That’s essentially F#’s own list.


The Week 3 recipe was always “one rule per case of the type”. Week 6: trees, the same way.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Nested patterns
let rec sumKnown xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> 0
    | Some x :: rest -> x + sumKnown rest
    | None :: rest -> sumKnown rest

let rec countBigCircles shapes =
    match shapes with
    | [] -> 0
    | Circle r :: rest when r > 1.0 -> 1 + countBigCircles rest
    | _ :: rest -> countBigCircles rest


One pattern checks the shape and takes it apart, several levels deep.

title: Modeling Data: Records, Unions, and Option
text:
Summary

Records: named fields, { x with … }, compared by content; annotate on clashes
Unions: one of several cases, each with its own data; constructors are patterns
FS0025 names the case you missed: every one is a bug
Count values: products multiply, sums add. Design out impossible states
option: absence in the type; handle None; never a magic value
F#’s list is a recursive union; “one rule per case”

title: Week 4 · Lab

Rules

Still no List module: list functions by recursion. From Week 5 on, the library is yours.
Every match complete; no FS0025 warnings.
Avoid _ for union cases you could name. A wildcard hides future cases from the compiler (see drill F3).
Never a magic value (0, -1, "") for “no answer”: return an option.
No mutable, no loops. Don’t change the types or the tests.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Predict: coming from Python
In Python, [1, 2] is a list of two numbers. In F#:
> [1, 2];;

val it: (int * int) list = [(1, 2)]
A list with one element: the pair (1, 2). No error, no warning.


In F#, the comma always makes a tuple. Lists use ;.

Ask for the type before revealing. Many will say “int list”. Emphasise: always read the type FSI reports.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
section: The list gives you the cases
text:
The list gives you the cases

Type — usually 'a list -> …
Base case — the empty list []
Recursive case — x :: rest: trust f rest, combine with x
Check — trace a short list. Getting smaller is free: rest is shorter.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
section: Problem: the length of a list
text:
Problem: the length of a list
length [7; 8; 9] = 3, length [] = 0

Your turn. Type? Base case? Recursive case?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
length: the recipe

Type — 'a list -> int: any element type
Base case — length [] = 0
Recursive case — one more than length rest
Check — length [7; 8] = 1 + (1 + 0) = 2


let rec length xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> 0
    | _ :: rest -> 1 + length rest


It never looks at the elements (_), so it is generic.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
sum: same recipe, another step
sum [1; 2; 3] = 6

Before the code: what is the base case? What is the recursive step?

Base case — sum [] = 0
Recursive step — add x to the trusted sum rest



let rec sum xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> 0
    | x :: rest -> x + sum rest


sum [1; 2; 3] = 1 + sum [2; 3]
              = 1 + (2 + sum [3])
              = 1 + (2 + (3 + sum []))
              = 1 + (2 + (3 + 0)) = 6

Give students a moment at “Before the code”. Ask what the base case should be, and why it is 0 and not 1.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
section: append: now the base case changes
text:
append: now the base case changes
append [1; 2] [3; 4] = [1; 2; 3; 4]

Before the code: there are two lists. Which one do you take apart? What is append [] ys?

Base case — append [] ys = ys: not []!
Recursive step — put x in front of the trusted append rest ys



let rec append xs ys =
    match xs with
    | [] -> ys
    | x :: rest -> x :: append rest ys


append [1; 2] [3; 4] = 1 :: append [2] [3; 4]
                     = 1 :: (2 :: append [] [3; 4])
                     = [1; 2; 3; 4]

Point out: only the first list is taken apart; the second is shared. Built in as @.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
section: isMember: now the answer is a bool
text:
isMember: now the answer is a bool
isMember 3 [1; 2; 3] = true, isMember 9 [1; 2] = false

Before the code: base case? Recursive step? Does it need to look at the whole list?

Base case — isMember x [] = false: nothing is in the empty list
Recursive step — x is the head, or it is in the trusted isMember x rest



let rec isMember x xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> false
    | y :: rest -> x = y || isMember x rest


|| stops as soon as the answer is true.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Shape 3: combine all
let rec maximum xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> failwith "maximum: empty list"
    | [x] -> x
    | x :: rest -> max x (maximum rest)

The maximum of no numbers doesn’t exist: base case [x], and [] is an error.


sum, length, product too: the base case is the answer for no elements (0, 0, 1).

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns

Problem: are all elements positive?
allPositive [1; 2] = true, allPositive [1; -2; 3] = false

Your turn. And: does your version look at the 3?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Shape 4: stop early
let rec allPositive xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> true
    | x :: rest -> x > 0 && allPositive rest

&& doesn’t evaluate its right side when the left is false (Week 1).
So allPositive [1; -2; 3; 4; 5] stops at -2. isMember has the same shape, with ||.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:

stutter [1; 2] = [1; 1; 2; 2]
concat [[1]; []; [2; 3]] = [1; 2; 3]

Your turn. How many elements does each x contribute?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Shape 5: each to many
let rec stutter xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> []
    | x :: rest -> x :: x :: stutter rest

let rec concat xss =
    match xss with
    | [] -> []
    | xs :: rest -> append xs (concat rest)


Each element contributes zero, one, or several elements. Other languages call this shape flatMap. Remember the name.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Why the shapes matter


Transform each
| x :: rest ->
    2 * x :: f rest
| x :: rest ->
    w.Length :: f rest

Keep some
| x :: rest when x % 2 = 0 -> …
| x :: rest when x = y -> …


In each shape, everything is the same except one small piece.


Week 5: each shape becomes one function; the piece becomes a parameter. You will recognise them all.

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns

Problem: pair up two lists
zip [1; 2; 3] ["a"; "b"] = [(1, "a"); (2, "b")]

Your turn. You need to look at both lists at once. How?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Matching on two values
let rec zip xs ys =
    match xs, ys with
    | x :: xs', y :: ys' -> (x, y) :: zip xs' ys'
    | _ -> []                     // either one ran out

match xs, ys with matches the pair (xs, ys): each rule has a pair of patterns.


val zip: xs: 'a list -> ys: 'b list -> ('a * 'b) list

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
Problem: unzip
unzip [(1, "a"); (2, "b")] = ([1; 2], ["a"; "b"])

Your turn. Trust unzip rest. What does it give you, and what do you do with it?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
section: Using the result of the recursive call
text:
Using the result of the recursive call
let rec unzip pairs =
    match pairs with
    | [] -> ([], [])
    | (x, y) :: rest ->
        let (xs, ys) = unzip rest     // trust it; take it apart
        (x :: xs, y :: ys)

Take the recursive result apart with a pattern, then build the answer.


let rec sumProd xs =
    match xs with
    | [] -> (0, 1)
    | x :: rest ->
        let (s, p) = sumProd rest
        (x + s, x * p)

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
A lookup table
let rec lookup key table =
    match table with
    | [] -> failwith ("lookup: no entry for " + key)
    | (k, v) :: _ when k = key -> v
    | _ :: rest -> lookup key rest

lookup "tea" prices = 45. The pattern (k, v) :: _ takes apart the first pair inside the list pattern.

Your turn. What if one list is empty? Otherwise, what goes first?

title: Lists, Tuples, and Recursion Patterns
text:
merge
let rec merge xs ys =
    match xs, ys with
    | [], ys -> ys
    | xs, [] -> xs
    | x :: xs', y :: ys' ->
        if x <= y then x :: merge xs' ys
        else y :: merge xs ys'

Each call removes one element from one of the lists, so it stops.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
section: A definition in terms of itself

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
rec is required
> let fact n = if n = 0 then 1 else n * fact (n - 1);;

error FS0039: The value or constructor 'fact' is not defined.

Without rec, the name isn’t bound yet inside its own body.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Tracing factIf 3
factIf 3 = 3 * factIf 2
         = 3 * (2 * factIf 1)
         = 3 * (2 * (1 * factIf 0))
         = 3 * (2 * (1 * 1))
         = 3 * (2 * 1)
         = 3 * 2
         = 6

The expression grows, then shrinks. The multiplications wait, kept on the call stack (Week 7).

Point at the widest line: three multiplications waiting. Ask: where does the computer keep them?

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Four steps, every time

Type — what goes in, what comes out
Base case — the input so small the answer is obvious
Recursive case — assume it works for a smaller input; build from that
Check — trace a small input; does every call get closer to the base case?


Step 3 feels like cheating. Trust the smaller call, the way you trust sqrt.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
The recipe on sumTo
Add up 1 + 2 + … + n.


Type — int -> int




Base case — sumTo 0 = 0




Recursive case — if sumTo (n - 1) is right, then sumTo n = n + sumTo (n - 1)




Check — sumTo 3 = 3 + (2 + (1 + 0)) = 6; each call subtracts 1



let rec sumToIf n =
    if n = 0 then 0
    else n + sumToIf (n - 1)

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
The math, and the code
The definition, written as cases:

\begin{aligned}
0! &= 1 \\
n! &= n \times (n-1)!
\end{aligned}


F# can say exactly this:
let rec fact n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 1
    | n -> n * fact (n - 1)


The definition you write on paper, typed in almost as it is.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
How match works
let rec fact n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 1
    | n -> n * fact (n - 1)


each | pattern -> expression is a rule
rules are tried top to bottom; the first that fits wins
a name pattern (n) fits anything, and binds the value



Rule 7: evaluate the value; try patterns in order; bind names; continue with that rule.

text:
Guards: a condition on a rule
sign n should be -1, 0, or 1. But “all positive numbers” is not one value…

let sign n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | n when n > 0 -> 1     // guard: only if n > 0
    | _ -> -1


The rule applies only if the pattern fits and the guard is true.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: powers
Compute x^n, for a float x and a natural number n.

power 2.0 3 = 8.0
power 1.5 2 = 2.25


Your turn. Type? Base case? Recursive case? Check?

Give 2–3 minutes, in pairs if possible. Collect the type first, then the base case. Resist showing the next slide until someone proposes the recursive case.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
power: the recipe

Type — float -> int -> float
Base case — x^0 = 1
Recursive case — x^n = x \times x^{n-1}
Check — power 2.0 3 = 2.0 * (2.0 * (2.0 * 1.0)) = 8.0


let rec power x n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 1.0
    | n -> x * power x (n - 1)


Two parameters, but only n shrinks; x is passed along unchanged.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: repeating text
Repeat a string n times.

repeat "ab" 3 = "ababab"
repeat "ab" 0 = ""


Your turn. Type? Base case? Recursive case? Check?

The base case is the interesting question: what is “zero copies” of a string?

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
repeat: the recipe

Type — string -> int -> string
Base case — zero copies is the empty string ""
Recursive case — one copy of s, followed by n - 1 copies
Check — repeat "ab" 2 = "ab" + ("ab" + "") = "abab"


let rec repeat s n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> ""
    | n -> s + repeat s (n - 1)


Recursion isn’t only arithmetic: anything built piece by piece.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: binary digits
Write a natural number in base 2, as a string.

binary 6 = "110"
binary 13 = "1101"


Your turn. Type? Base case? Recursive case? Check?


Hint: the last binary digit of n is n % 2. What are the digits before it?

Show the hint only if the room is stuck after a couple of minutes. Many students will find one base case (0); leave the second for the next slides.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
binary: the recipe

Type — int -> string
Base cases — 0 is "0", and 1 is "1"
Recursive case — the digits of n / 2, then the last digit n % 2
Check — binary 6 = binary 3 + "0" = (binary 1 + "1") + "0" = "110"


let rec binary n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> "0"
    | 1 -> "1"
    | n -> binary (n / 2) + string (n % 2)


“Smaller” here means halving, not subtracting 1.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Predict: one base case only
With only | 0 -> "0" as the base case, what is binary 6?

binary 6 = binary 3 + "0"
         = (binary 1 + "1") + "0"
         = ((binary 0 + "1") + "1") + "0"
         = "0110"
A leading zero. That is why binary needs two base cases.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: adding up digits
Add up the decimal digits of a natural number.

digitSum 1234 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10
digitSum 7 = 7


Your turn. Type? Base case? Recursive case? Check?


Hint: n % 10 is the last digit; n / 10 is the number without it.

Watch for the base case: most students first write | 0 -> 0, which also works. Ask whether a one-digit base case is more natural, and how to write “any number below 10” as a pattern (guard).

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
digitSum: the recipe

Type — int -> int
Base case — a number below 10 is its own digit sum: a range, so a guard
Recursive case — the last digit, plus the digit sum of the rest
Check — digitSum 1234 = 4 + (3 + (2 + 1)) = 10: each call removes one digit


let rec digitSum n =
    match n with
    | n when n < 10 -> n
    | n -> n % 10 + digitSum (n / 10)

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: greatest common divisor
The largest number that divides both a and b.

gcd 48 18 = 6
gcd 17 5 = 1


Euclid’s fact (around 300 BC): \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b,\ a \bmod b)


Your turn. With that fact, what is the base case? Write it.

Euclid’s fact is given, since it’s number theory rather than programming. The programming question is the base case: what happens when b reaches 0?

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
gcd: the recipe

Type — int -> int -> int
Base case — \gcd(a, 0) = a: everything divides 0
Recursive case — Euclid’s fact
Check — the second argument shrinks: a % b is always less than b


let rec gcd a b =
    match b with
    | 0 -> a
    | b -> gcd b (a % b)


gcd 48 18 = gcd 18 12 = gcd 12 6 = gcd 6 0 = 6

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
gcd vs fact
fact 3 = 3 * (2 * (1 * fact 0))       work waits: the expression grows

gcd 48 18 = gcd 18 12 = gcd 12 6      nothing waits: it never grows

Remember this difference. It becomes important in Week 7.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Problem: Fibonacci numbers
0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …: each is the sum of the two before it.

fib 0 = 0, fib 1 = 1
fib 10 = 55


Your turn. Type? Base case(s)? Recursive case?

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
fib: the recipe

Type — int -> int
Base cases — fib 0 = 0 and fib 1 = 1: two, because the recursive case looks two steps back
Recursive case — fib n = fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2): two recursive calls
Check — fib 4 = fib 3 + fib 2 = (fib 2 + fib 1) + (fib 1 + fib 0) = … = 3


let rec fib n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | 1 -> 1
    | n -> fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)


It reads exactly like the definition.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Is fib fast?
Your turn. How long will fib 40 take? And fib 42?

> fib 40;;
Real: 00:00:01.002 ...
> fib 42;;
Real: 00:00:02.254 ...


About ×1.6 per step: the same values are computed over and over. Correct, but a bad program.

Before revealing the timings, ask for guesses: how long will fib 40 take? Then ask why it’s slow; drill A7 draws the call tree.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
section: No way to the base case
text:
No way to the base case
What does fact (-1) do?

It counts down forever: -1, -2, -3, …
Stack overflow.
Repeated 261720 times:
   at FSI_0001.fact(Int32)


Same crash if the call doesn’t shrink (fact n), or the base case is unreachable (FS0026).


let rec factSafe n =
    match n with
    | n when n < 0 -> failwith "factSafe: negative input"
    | 0 -> 1
    | n -> n * factSafe (n - 1)

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Numbers that are too big
> fact 12;;
val it: int = 479001600

> fact 13;;
val it: int = 1932053504
Is this right?

13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800, but int stops at about 2.1 \times 10^9 and wraps silently.


Use int64 (literals 20L) or bigint (literals 20I).

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Find the bug
let rec repeat s n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> s
    | n -> s + repeat s (n - 1)

repeat "ab" 2 gives "ababab": an off-by-one, with no warning at all.


Step 4 of the recipe, tracing a small input, is what catches it.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Many arrows
> let add x y = x + y;;
val add: x: int -> y: int -> int

Arrows group to the right: int -> (int -> int)


Give it one argument, get a function back:
let add x y = x + y
let add5 = add 5              // a function still waiting for y
let eight = add5 3


Application groups to the left: add 5 3 = (add 5) 3. This is currying.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Partial application
let twoTo = power 2.0         // int -> float: powers of two
let kilo = twoTo 10           // 1024.0

let say = printfn "Hello, %s!"   // string -> unit


The Week 1 promise: printfn "…%s…" is a function waiting for a string, checked at compile time.


Order matters: put the “setting” parameters first, the data last.

title: Functions, Recursion, and Reading Types
text:
Generic types
let identity x = x
let first x y = x
let alwaysZero _ = 0
val identity: x: 'a -> 'a
val first: x: 'a -> y: 'b -> 'a
val alwaysZero: 'a -> int

'a means any type. And 'a -> 'a knows nothing about its argument, so it can only hand it back.

text:
Working out a type by hand

Unknowns — a placeholder for each parameter and the result
Clues — each use of a parameter says something
Combine — disagreeing clues are a type error
Generalise — no clues at all? It stays 'a


let pick x y = if x > 0 then y + 1 else y * 2



x > 0: x is int
y + 1: y is int, and so is the result



pick: x: int -> y: int -> int

By the end of today you can:

run F# in FSI and in scripts
read what FSI tells you: name, type, value
write values and functions with let
explain why if … then … else produces a value
evaluate a program by hand, step by step
explain why mutation makes programs harder to reason about


Set expectations: we go slowly this week on purpose. Everything later rests on the substitution model.

title: Programs as Expressions
section: You have already met functional ideas
text:
You have already met functional ideas

Lambdas, under many names: Java/C# lambdas, C++ lambdas, JS arrow functions, Python lambda. Every callback is a function used as a value
React: components as pure functions of props; state updates create new objects
Rust: immutable by default; blocks are expressions
Java, C#, Kotlin, TypeScript, Python: records, pattern matching, tagged unions
LINQ, Java streams, JS map/filter/reduce: functional collection processing


This course: learn these ideas where they are clearest (F#), then carry them anywhere.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Statement style: how
// Statement style: create a variable, then change it step by step.
let mutable total = 0
total <- total + 72
total <- total + 85
total <- total + 90
let mutable average = 0.0
average <- float total / 3.0

To know what average is, you replay the steps in order.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Expression style: what
// Expression style: say what the average IS.
let averageOf3 a b c = float (a + b + c) / 3.0
let myAverage = averageOf3 72 85 90










Imperative
Functional




a program is
statements that change state
expressions that define values


a variable is
a box whose contents change
a name for a value that never changes


to understand it
replay the steps
replace names by their meaning

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Talking to FSI
> 2 * 3 + 4;;
val it: int = 10


val: here is a value
it: the name FSI gives the last result
int: its type
10: its value



;; means “evaluate now”. It is only used in FSI, never in files.

title: Programs as Expressions
section: let binds a name to a value
text:
let binds a name to a value
let price = 25 * 5
let newPrice = 2 * price
let isExpensive = newPrice > 500

The environment after these three lines:
[ price ↦ 125,   newPrice ↦ 250,   isExpensive ↦ false ]


No types written, all types known: type inference.

title: Programs as Expressions
Programs as Expressions
text:
if produces a value
let temperature = 34
let advice =
    if temperature > 30 then "Stay hydrated"
    else "Enjoy the weather"
let describe t =
    if t > 35 then "very hot"
    elif t > 30 then "hot"
    elif t > 20 then "pleasant"
    else "cool"

So: both branches need the same type, and the else is required.

title: Programs as Expressions
section: The compiler says it for us
text:
The compiler says it for us
> if 3 > 2 then "yes";;

error FS0001: This 'if' expression is missing an 'else' branch.
Because 'if' is an expression, and not a statement, add an 'else'
branch which also returns a value of type 'string'.

title: Programs as Expressions
section: A block’s value is its last expression
text:
A block’s value is its last expression
let totalWithVat price quantity =
    let subtotal = price * quantity   // local binding
    let vat = subtotal * 7 / 100      // Thai VAT: 7%
    subtotal + vat                    // the result


let lines are local: visible only below them
no return: the last line is the result
indentation decides what belongs to the body

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
But what about printfn?
If everything is an expression… what is printfn "Hello"?

It is an expression. Evaluating it:

produces the value (), of type unit
and prints, which is a side effect

> let greet name = printfn "Hello, %s!" name;;
val greet: name: string -> unit

Let students propose answers first. Someone usually says “printfn is a statement”; the FSI response shows it has a type and a value.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Two different properties









Means
Guaranteed by F#?




Everything is an expression
every construct has a value and a type
yes, by design


Pure
evaluating it does nothing but produce its value
no, it’s our discipline




2 + 3 is pure. printfn "Hi" is not.


This course: build programs mostly from pure expressions, and keep effects few, visible, and at the edges.

title: Programs as Expressions
section: Effects happen once, when evaluated, in order
text:
Effects happen once, when evaluated, in order
let u = printfn "computing..."   // prints now, once
let v = u                        // u is just (), nothing is printed

let answer () =
    printfn "thinking..."        // evaluated first, for its effect
    printfn "almost there..."    // then this one
    42                           // the value of the whole block


Lines before the last run top to bottom for their effects, and their values are thrown away. -> unit in a type is a warning sign: expect an effect.

Type
Values

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
No mixing int and float
> 2 * 3.0;;
error FS0001: The type 'float' does not match the type 'int'

Convert explicitly, using the type’s name as a function:
let items = 3
let unitPrice = 19.5
let cost = float items * unitPrice   // float 3 is 3.0
let rounded = int 57.9               // truncates: 57

Mention the F# 6 nuance only if asked: an int is widened when a float is already expected (passing an argument to a float parameter). Operators never mix.

title: Programs as Expressions
Programs as Expressions
text:
Defining and applying
let circleArea r = System.Math.PI * r * r
let area1 = circleArea 1.0
let area2 = circleArea 2.5
val circleArea: r: float -> float

Apply by writing the argument after the function, no parentheses needed.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Parentheses only group
let square x = x * x

let a1 = square 3 + 1        // (square 3) + 1 = 10
let a2 = square (3 + 1)      // square 4       = 16

Function application binds tighter than any operator.


With nothing to say otherwise, x * x assumes int, so square: x: int -> int.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Two parameters
let totalCost unitPrice quantity = unitPrice * float quantity
let order = totalCost 19.5 4
val totalCost: unitPrice: float -> quantity: int -> float







Not totalCost(19.5, 4)


(19.5, 4) is one value, a pair. Write totalCost 19.5 4.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Functions are values
let double = fun x -> 2 * x     // same as: let double x = 2 * x
let eight = (fun x -> 2 * x) 4  // apply it directly

fun x -> … is a function without a name, a lambda.
A function can be bound, passed, and returned like any value. That is Week 5.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
The rules

Name — replace it by the value it is bound to
Arguments — evaluate them to values first
Apply — take the body; replace each parameter by its argument
Operator — compute it once both sides are values
if — evaluate the condition; keep only the chosen branch
Local let — evaluate it; replace the name in the lines below

We write ⇝ for “evaluates in one step to”.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Tracing sumOfSquares 3 (1 + 1)
let square x = x * x
let sumOfSquares a b = square a + square b
   sumOfSquares 3 (1 + 1)
⇝ sumOfSquares 3 2              (2) arguments first
⇝ square 3 + square 2           (3) a ↦ 3, b ↦ 2
⇝ (3 * 3) + square 2            (3) x ↦ 3
⇝ 9 + square 2                  (4)
⇝ 9 + (2 * 2)                   (3) x ↦ 2
⇝ 9 + 4                         (4)
⇝ 13                            (4)

Every line is an F# expression. Every line has the same value.

Each click reveals one step. Before each click, ask which rule applies next.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Tracing with if
let shippingFee weight =
    if weight <= 1 then 40
    elif weight <= 5 then 40 + (weight - 1) * 15
    else 100 + (weight - 5) * 10
   shippingFee 3
⇝ if 3 <= 1 then 40                               (3)
   elif 3 <= 5 then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15
   else 100 + (3 - 5) * 10
⇝ if false then 40 elif 3 <= 5 then …             (4)
⇝ if 3 <= 5 then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15 else …         (5)
⇝ if true then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15 else …           (4)
⇝ 40 + (3 - 1) * 15                               (5)
⇝ 40 + 2 * 15  ⇝  40 + 30                         (4)
⇝ 70                                              (4)

Point out that the unchosen branches are never evaluated.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Why this works

Anywhere a name appears, you can replace it by its definition. Anywhere an expression appears, you can replace it by its value. The meaning does not change.


This property is called referential transparency.


It lets you understand each piece of a program on its own, the way you simplify one part of an equation.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
When substitution breaks
let mutable counter = 0
let nextId () =
    counter <- counter + 1
    counter

let x1 = nextId () + nextId ()   // 1 + 2 = 3
let x2 = 2 * nextId ()           // 2 * 3 = 6

In mathematics, f(x) + f(x) = 2\,f(x) for every f and x.
Here, with x = (): 3 ≠ 6.


nextId () has no fixed value. To understand it, you are back to replaying steps.


Every side effect does this: printfn "Hi" has value (), but replacing it by () removes the output. DateTime.Now differs each time you read it.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Two names, one array
let scores = [| 70; 80; 90 |]   // an array: mutable
let backup = scores             // NOT a copy!
scores[0] <- 0
let surprise = backup[0]        // 0: backup changed too

let backup = scores gives the same array a second name. This is aliasing.


If nothing can change, sharing is always safe: pass it anywhere, store it, share it between threads (Week 12).

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Mutation: available, but explicit

F# values are immutable by default; “change” means compute a new value
let mutable and <- exist, for when you can say why


> let mutable x = 1;;
> x = 2;;
val it: bool = false
= compares. <- assigns.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Beyond F#









Value-producing if
Non-reassignable binding




Rust
let a = if t > 30 { "hot" } else { "ok" };
let (vs let mut)


Kotlin
val a = if (t > 30) "hot" else "ok"
val


TypeScript
const a = t > 30 ? "hot" : "ok";
const, binding only!


Python
a = "hot" if t > 30 else "ok"
none (convention)




Habit to keep: default to the non-reassignable form; make conditionals produce values; treat “update” as “compute a new value”.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Rewrite without mutable
let mutable msg = "Result: "
if score >= 50 then msg <- msg + "pass" else msg <- msg + "fail"
msg <- msg + $" ({score})"

let msgExpression score =
    let verdict = if score >= 50 then "pass" else "fail"
    $"Result: {verdict} ({score})"
Naming the intermediate value is often the cleanest rewrite.

title: Programs as Expressions
text:
Summary

Programs are expressions; functions map values to values
let binds; bindings never change (shadowing makes a new one)
if is an expression: same type in both branches, else required
Apply with spaces: f x y; parentheses only group
No mutation ⇒ evaluate by substitution (referential transparency)
Immutable values can be shared safely

title: Functional Programming

title: Week 1 · Drills
text:
Work through these on paper first, then check in FSI. The point is to build the habit of predicting what F# will do. Being wrong and finding out why is exactly the learning. Answers are hidden under each section; open them only after you have committed to an answer.

A. Predict the FSI response
For each input, write what FSI replies: the type and value, or error together with a one-line reason. Do not run them first.

7 / 2;;
7.0 / 2.0;;
7 % 2;;
"7" + "2";;
"7" + 2;;
sqrt 16;;
sqrt 16.0;;
float 7 / 2.0;;
int 3.99;;
string 42 + "!";;
let y = 10;; followed by y = 11;;
not (3 < 2) && "abc" < "abd";;
(fun x -> x * 3) 5;;
if 2 > 1 then 10 else "twenty";;







TipAnswers






val it: int = 3, integer division drops the remainder.
val it: float = 3.5
val it: int = 1, the remainder.
val it: string = "72", + joins strings.
Error: int does not match string. F# does not convert 2 to "2" for you.
Error: int does not support Sqrt. sqrt needs a float.
val it: float = 4.0
val it: float = 3.5. float 7 is 7.0, and function application binds tighter than /.
val it: int = 3, conversion truncates; it does not round.
val it: string = "42!"
val y: int = 10, then val it: bool = false. = compares; it never assigns.
val it: bool = true. Strings compare alphabetically, and "abc" comes before "abd".
val it: int = 15
Error: all branches of an if must have the same type.






B. Read the type
Without running them, write the type FSI will report for each function. Then explain in words what the type tells you.
let f x = x + 1
let g x = x + 1.0
let h x = x + "!"
let k x y = x * y + 1
let greet name = printfn "Hello, %s" name
let describe n = if n % 2 = 0 then "even" else "odd"






TipAnswers






f: x: int -> int, because 1 is an int, so x must be one too.
g: x: float -> float, because 1.0 is a float.
h: x: string -> string, because "!" is a string, so + here means joining strings.
k: x: int -> y: int -> int: two int parameters, int result.
greet: name: string -> unit. It returns nothing interesting; it is used for its side effect (printing).
describe: n: int -> string. % and = 0 force n to be an int, and both branches are strings.

In every case F# found the type from how the parameter is used. Week 2 looks at this closely.





C. Trace by hand
Use these definitions:
let square x = x * x
let rectangleArea width height = width * height

let shippingFee weight =
    if weight <= 1 then 40
    elif weight <= 5 then 40 + (weight - 1) * 15
    else 100 + (weight - 5) * 10

let priceAfterDiscount price qty =
    let subtotal = price * qty
    let discount = if subtotal > 1000 then subtotal / 10 else 0
    subtotal - discount
Evaluate each expression step by step using the substitution rules from the notes (number each step with the rule you used), until you reach a value.

rectangleArea 2 (1 + 2)
square (square 2)
shippingFee 7
priceAfterDiscount 300 4. Then, without a full trace, what is priceAfterDiscount 300 3, and why?







TipAnswers





1.   rectangleArea 2 (1 + 2)
   ⇝ rectangleArea 2 3             (2)
   ⇝ 2 * 3                         (3) width ↦ 2, height ↦ 3
   ⇝ 6                             (4)

2.   square (square 2)
   ⇝ square (2 * 2)                (2),(3) the argument first: x ↦ 2
   ⇝ square 4                      (4)
   ⇝ 4 * 4                         (3) x ↦ 4
   ⇝ 16                            (4)

3.   shippingFee 7
   ⇝ if 7 <= 1 then 40 elif 7 <= 5 then … else 100 + (7 - 5) * 10    (3)
   ⇝ if false then 40 elif 7 <= 5 then … else …                      (4)
   ⇝ if 7 <= 5 then 40 + (7 - 1) * 15 else 100 + (7 - 5) * 10        (5)
   ⇝ if false then … else 100 + (7 - 5) * 10                         (4)
   ⇝ 100 + (7 - 5) * 10                                              (5)
   ⇝ 100 + 2 * 10  ⇝  100 + 20  ⇝  120                               (4)

4.   priceAfterDiscount 300 4
   ⇝ let subtotal = 300 * 4                                   (3)
     let discount = if subtotal > 1000 then subtotal / 10 else 0
     subtotal - discount
   ⇝ let discount = if 1200 > 1000 then 1200 / 10 else 0      (6) subtotal ↦ 1200
     1200 - discount
   ⇝ let discount = 1200 / 10                                 (4),(5)
     1200 - discount
   ⇝ 1200 - 120                                               (6) discount ↦ 120
   ⇝ 1080                                                     (4)
For priceAfterDiscount 300 3: the subtotal is 900, which is not above 1000, so the if chooses 0 and the result is 900.
Note in trace 2 that the inner square 2 is evaluated before the outer square is applied. That is rule (2): arguments first.





D. From statements to expressions
Each snippet below is written in statement style, using a mutable variable. Rewrite it as a single binding with no mutable and no <-. Then answer the question.
D1.
let mutable fee = 0
if isMember then fee <- 50 else fee <- 100
D2.
let mutable msg = "Result: "
if score >= 50 then msg <- msg + "pass" else msg <- msg + "fail"
msg <- msg + $" ({score})"
D3.
let mutable category = ""
if bmi < 18.5 then category <- "under"
if bmi >= 18.5 && bmi < 25.0 then category <- "normal"
if bmi >= 25.0 then category <- "over"
Question: The statement version needs a placeholder "". What goes wrong if one of the three conditions has a typo, say bmi > 25.0 instead of bmi >= 25.0? Could the same mistake happen silently in your expression version?






TipAnswers





let feeExpression isMember = if isMember then 50 else 100
let msgExpression score =
    let verdict = if score >= 50 then "pass" else "fail"
    $"Result: {verdict} ({score})"
Naming the intermediate value (verdict) is often the cleanest way to turn a sequence of updates into expressions.
let categoryExpression bmi =
    if bmi < 18.5 then "under"
    elif bmi < 25.0 then "normal"
    else "over"
With the typo, a BMI of exactly 25.0 matches none of the conditions, so category stays "". Nothing warns you, and the empty string escapes into the rest of the program. In the expression version, the final else covers every remaining case, and F# requires it. Because each branch only has to handle what the earlier ones didn’t, overlapping or missing ranges are much harder to write by accident.





E. Can you substitute?
For each pair, say whether the two versions are guaranteed to behave the same, and why. Assume square, shippingFee, and greet are as defined in the notes, and nextId is the counter function from the notes.

square 5 + square 5 and 2 * square 5
nextId () + nextId () and 2 * nextId ()
shippingFee 3 + shippingFee 3 and
let t = shippingFee 3
t + t
Calling greet "Ann" twice in a row, and
let g = greet "Ann"
g
g
System.DateTime.Now - System.DateTime.Now and
let t = System.DateTime.Now
t - t







TipAnswers






Same. square 5 always means 25, so both are 50.
Different. nextId () changes a mutable variable, so each call gives a different result (3 vs 6, starting from 0).
Same. shippingFee only computes; binding its result to a name and using it twice changes nothing.
Different, even though both produce the value (). The first prints Hello, Ann! twice. In the second, greet "Ann" runs once, when g is bound; after that, g is just the value () and mentioning it prints nothing.
Different. The second is always exactly zero. In the first, the clock is read twice, so the difference may be a tiny non-zero time. Or it may be zero, which is worse: the bug only shows up occasionally. Reading the clock is a side effect, even though nothing is printed or changed.

The pattern: substitution is safe for pure expressions, the ones that only compute. As soon as an expression does something (changes a variable, prints, reads input or the clock), how many times it runs, and when, starts to matter.





F. Spot and fix
Each line has a problem. Say what F# will report (or what goes wrong), then fix it.

let floor = rectangleArea(4, 3)
let total = 3 * 19.5
let sign x = if x > 0 then "positive"
let mutable counter = 5 followed by counter = 6 (the intent is to set it to 6)







TipAnswers






(4, 3) is one value, a pair (type int * int), but rectangleArea expects two separate ints. It is a type error.
int and float can’t be mixed in arithmetic. It is a type error.
The if produces a string, so it needs an else branch. It is an error.
There is no error, but counter = 6 compares and evaluates to false, so counter stays 5. At the top level of a script this happens silently. Inside a function body, F# warns you (FS0020: The result of this equality expression has type 'bool' and is implicitly discarded… If you intended to mutate a value, then use the '<-' operator).

let f1 = rectangleArea 4 3              // F1
let f2 = float 3 * 19.5                 // F2
let sign x = if x > 0 then "positive" else "not positive"   // F3
let mutable counter = 5
counter <- 6                            // F4

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
section: 4.1 let binds a name to a value
text:
4.1 let binds a name to a value
let price = 25 * 5
let newPrice = 2 * price
let isExpensive = newPrice > 500
In FSI:
> let price = 25 * 5;;
val price: int = 125

> let newPrice = 2 * price;;
val newPrice: int = 250

> let isExpensive = newPrice > 500;;
val isExpensive: bool = false
let price = 25 * 5 does two things: it evaluates the expression 25 * 5 to the value 125, and it binds the name price to that value. We write the binding as
price ↦ 125
and read it as “price is bound to 125”. The collection of all bindings currently in effect is called the environment. After the three declarations above, the environment contains:
[ price ↦ 125,   newPrice ↦ 250,   isExpensive ↦ false ]
When F# evaluates 2 * price, it looks price up in the environment and finds 125.
Notice that we never wrote a type. F# worked out that price is an int because 25 * 5 is an int. This is called type inference. The types are still there, and they are checked strictly; you just don’t have to write most of them. Week 2 looks at type inference more closely.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
4.2 A binding does not change
In FSI you are allowed to type let with a name that already exists:
> let rate = 7;;
val rate: int = 7

> let addTax amount = amount + amount * rate / 100;;
val addTax: amount: int -> int

> let rate = 10;;
val rate: int = 10

> addTax 100;;
val it: int = 107
If let rate = 10 had changed rate, then addTax 100 would give 110. It gives 107. The second let created a new binding that happens to use the same name. From then on, the name rate refers to the new binding, but addTax was defined earlier and still refers to the old one. This is called shadowing: the new binding hides the old one; it does not modify it.
The same thing happens inside a function or a block, where re-using a name is also allowed:
let taxDemo =
    let rate = 7
    let addTax amount = amount + amount * rate / 100   // uses rate = 7
    let rate = 10                                      // a NEW binding named rate
    addTax 100                                         // still 107, not 110






WarningFSI vs script files



Re-using a top-level name works in an FSI session because each thing you type is treated as a separate step. In a script file, two top-level let rate = … lines are an error (Duplicate definition of value 'rate'). Shadowing is still allowed inside functions and blocks. In practice, avoid re-using names at the top level anyway; it makes code harder to read.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
section: 5.1 Blocks: the last expression is the result
text:
5.1 Blocks: the last expression is the result
A function body can span several lines. Lines that start with let introduce local bindings, visible only in the lines below them. The last line is an expression, and its value is the result of the whole block:
let totalWithVat price quantity =
    let subtotal = price * quantity   // local binding
    let vat = subtotal * 7 / 100      // Thai VAT: 7%
    subtotal + vat                    // the result
There is no return keyword. The body of totalWithVat is an expression, and subtotal + vat is its final part.






ImportantIndentation matters



F# uses indentation to decide what belongs to what. Everything in the body of totalWithVat must be indented more than let totalWithVat, and the lines of the body must line up with each other. Use spaces, not tabs (your editor will do this for you).

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
5.2 But what about printfn?
Here is a fair question. If everything is an expression that produces a value, what is printfn "Hello"? It clearly does something: it prints.
The answer is that printfn "Hello" is an expression, and evaluating it has two results:

it produces a value: (), pronounced “unit”, the only value of the type unit;
while it is being evaluated, it prints. Something happens in the world beyond producing the value. That is called a side effect.

let greet name =
    printfn "Hello, %s!" name    // printfn returns () : unit

let greeting = greet "Somchai"   // greeting : unit = ()
> let greet name = printfn "Hello, %s!" name;;
val greet: name: string -> unit
So two different properties are easy to mix up:








Property
What it means
Does F# guarantee it?




Everything is an expression
Every construct produces a value with a type, even if the value is just (). There are no statements.
Yes. It is how the language is built.


Pure
Evaluating the expression does nothing except produce its value: no printing, no changing variables, no reading input or files.
No. 2 + 3 is pure; printfn "Hello" is not. Keeping code pure is our discipline.



This course is largely about the second property: writing as much of a program as possible out of pure expressions, and keeping the side effects few, visible, and at the edges.

5.2.1 Effects happen when an expression is evaluated
A side effect happens at the moment its expression is evaluated, and only then:
let u = printfn "computing..."   // prints now, once
let v = u                        // u is just (), nothing is printed
> let u = printfn "computing...";;
computing...
val u: unit = ()

> u;;
val it: unit = ()
The message is printed once, when u is bound. After that, u is just the value (), and using it prints nothing. The value was kept; the effect was not.


5.2.2 Blocks run their effects in order
This also explains how blocks work when they contain effects. The lines before the last are evaluated in order, top to bottom, only for their effects, and their values are thrown away. The last line gives the block its value:
let answer () =
    printfn "thinking..."        // evaluated first, for its effect
    printfn "almost there..."    // then this one
    42                           // the value of the whole block
> answer ();;
thinking...
almost there...
val it: int = 42
Since the values of the earlier lines are thrown away, they should be (). If one of them produces a real value, F# warns you, because a discarded value is usually a mistake:
> let bad () =
      42
      printfn "done";;

warning FS0020: The result of this expression has type 'int' and is implicitly
ignored. Consider using 'ignore' to discard this value explicitly, ...
val bad: unit -> unit
If you really do want to throw a value away, say so by passing it to ignore:
let logAndReturn x =
    printfn "value = %d" x
    x

logAndReturn 5 |> ignore         // we only wanted the printing
The |> symbol means “pass the value on the left into the function on the right”; we will use it a lot from Week 5.


5.2.3 unit in a type is a warning sign
Look again at greet: name: string -> unit. The type says: “give me a string, and I will give you back nothing interesting”. A function like that can only be useful because of what it does, never because of what it returns. So whenever you see -> unit at the end of a type, expect a side effect. (F# cannot stop you from hiding an effect inside a function that returns something else, like nextId below. The unit hint is only a hint.)






TipA small preview of Week 2



Try let say = printfn "Hello, %s!";; in FSI. Without the name argument, printfn "Hello, %s!" is already a function of type string -> unit, waiting for its string. F# even checks that the %s matches the argument you give it. Week 2 explains how this works.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
section: 6.1 Arithmetic never mixes int and float
text:
6.1 Arithmetic never mixes int and float
> 2 * 3.0;;

  2 * 3.0;;
  ----^^^

error FS0001: The type 'float' does not match the type 'int'
Many languages quietly convert 2 to 2.0 here. F# refuses, because silent conversions are a classic source of bugs. You convert explicitly, using the type name as a function:
let items = 3
let unitPrice = 19.5
let cost = float items * unitPrice   // float 3 is 3.0
let rounded = int 57.9               // truncates: 57
Similarly, int "42" turns a string into an int, and string 42 turns a number into a string.






NoteOne exception you will meet



Since F# 6, when the compiler already knows that a float is expected, for example when you pass an argument to a function whose parameter is a float, it will widen an int for you. So circleArea 2 works even though circleArea expects a float. Arithmetic operators still never mix the two: 2 * 3.0 and n + 1.5 (with n : int) are errors. When in doubt, write the conversion.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
6.2 Building strings
Put $ in front of a string to interpolate expressions inside {…}:
let student = "Ploy"
let score = 87
let report = $"{student} scored {score} points, {100 - score} short of full marks"
report is "Ploy scored 87 points, 13 short of full marks". Anything inside the braces is an ordinary F# expression.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
7.1 Defining and applying functions
let circleArea r = System.Math.PI * r * r
let area1 = circleArea 1.0
let area2 = circleArea 2.5
> let circleArea r = System.Math.PI * r * r;;
val circleArea: r: float -> float
let circleArea r = … declares a function named circleArea with one parameter r. FSI reports its type as r: float -> float: a function from float to float. F# inferred that r is a float because it is multiplied by System.Math.PI, which is a float.
To apply a function, write the function followed by its argument, separated by a space. No parentheses are needed:
circleArea 2.5
Parentheses are only for grouping. Function application binds more tightly than any operator, so:
let square x = x * x

let a1 = square 3 + 1        // (square 3) + 1 = 10
let a2 = square (3 + 1)      // square 4       = 16
square 3 + 1 means (square 3) + 1. If you want to square 3 + 1, you must say so with parentheses.






NoteWhen F# can’t tell which kind of number you mean



FSI reports square as x: int -> int. Nothing in x * x says whether x is an int or a float, and in that case F# assumes int. Compare circleArea, where System.Math.PI settles the question. Week 2 shows how to state the type yourself when you want something else.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
7.2 Functions with two parameters
A function can take several parameters, separated by spaces, and is applied the same way:
let totalCost unitPrice quantity = unitPrice * float quantity
let order = totalCost 19.5 4
> let totalCost unitPrice quantity = unitPrice * float quantity;;
val totalCost: unitPrice: float -> quantity: int -> float
The type float -> int -> float reads “takes a float, then an int, and produces a float”. F# worked out that quantity is an int because it is converted with float, and that unitPrice is a float because it is multiplied by a float. The repeated arrows are not an accident; in Week 2 we will see what they really mean, and why they are so useful. For now, read the last type as the result and everything before it as the parameters.






WarningDon’t write f(a, b)



In C or Java you would call totalCost(19.5, 4). In F#, (19.5, 4) is a single value, a pair (Week 3), so totalCost (19.5, 4) passes one argument and gives a type error (expected to have type 'float' but here has type 'float * int'). Write totalCost 19.5 4.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
7.3 Anonymous functions
A function does not need a name. fun x -> 2 * x is a function value, just as 42 is an integer value:
let double = fun x -> 2 * x     // same as: let double x = 2 * x
let eight = (fun x -> 2 * x) 4  // apply it directly
> fun s -> String.length s;;
val it: s: string -> int
let double x = 2 * x is simply a shorter way of writing let double = fun x -> 2 * x. A function is a value like any other: it can be bound to a name, passed to another function, or returned from one. Anonymous functions (also called lambdas) become essential from Week 5.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.1 The rules
To evaluate an expression, repeat until you reach a value:

Replace a name by the value it is bound to.
Evaluate the arguments of a function application to values first.
Apply a function by taking its body and replacing each parameter with the matching argument value.
Evaluate an operator (+, *, >, …) once both sides are values.
Evaluate an if by evaluating the condition, then keep only the chosen branch.
Evaluate a local let x = e in a block by evaluating e to a value v, then replacing x by v in the lines below it.

We write ⇝ for “evaluates in one step to”.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.2 A first trace
With these definitions:
let square x = x * x

let a1 = square 3 + 1        // (square 3) + 1 = 10
let a2 = square (3 + 1)      // square 4       = 16
let sumOfSquares a b = square a + square b
let’s evaluate sumOfSquares 3 (1 + 1):
   sumOfSquares 3 (1 + 1)
⇝ sumOfSquares 3 2              (2) evaluate the arguments
⇝ square 3 + square 2           (3) body of sumOfSquares, a ↦ 3, b ↦ 2
⇝ (3 * 3) + square 2            (3) body of square, x ↦ 3
⇝ 9 + square 2                  (4)
⇝ 9 + (2 * 2)                   (3) body of square, x ↦ 2
⇝ 9 + 4                         (4)
⇝ 13                            (4)
Every line is an ordinary F# expression, and every line has the same value, 13. Evaluation is just rewriting an expression into simpler expressions with the same meaning, until nothing is left to simplify.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.3 A trace with if
A courier charges by weight (in kg):
let shippingFee weight =
    if weight <= 1 then 40
    elif weight <= 5 then 40 + (weight - 1) * 15
    else 100 + (weight - 5) * 10
   shippingFee 3
⇝ if 3 <= 1 then 40                               (3) weight ↦ 3
   elif 3 <= 5 then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15
   else 100 + (3 - 5) * 10
⇝ if false then 40 elif 3 <= 5 then …             (4)
⇝ if 3 <= 5 then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15 else …         (5) drop the first branch
⇝ if true then 40 + (3 - 1) * 15 else …           (4)
⇝ 40 + (3 - 1) * 15                               (5) keep the chosen branch
⇝ 40 + 2 * 15                                     (4)
⇝ 40 + 30                                         (4)
⇝ 70                                              (4)
Notice that the branches that were not chosen are never evaluated. Only the condition decides.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.4 A trace with local bindings
Recall totalWithVat from earlier:
let totalWithVat price quantity =
    let subtotal = price * quantity   // local binding
    let vat = subtotal * 7 / 100      // Thai VAT: 7%
    subtotal + vat                    // the result
   totalWithVat 250 4
⇝ let subtotal = 250 * 4                  (3) price ↦ 250, quantity ↦ 4
   let vat = subtotal * 7 / 100
   subtotal + vat
⇝ let vat = 1000 * 7 / 100                (6) subtotal ↦ 1000
   1000 + vat
⇝ 1000 + 70                               (6) vat ↦ 70
⇝ 1070                                    (4)
(We skipped writing 250 * 4 ⇝ 1000 and 1000 * 7 / 100 ⇝ 70 as separate steps. Once you are comfortable, you may combine obvious arithmetic steps.)






TipTraces are a debugging tool



You will not write traces for every function you ever write. But when a function gives a result you don’t expect, tracing a small input by hand is often the fastest way to find out why. Many of this week’s drills are traces, so that the habit becomes automatic.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.5 The substitution rule, stated plainly
What makes this work is a simple property:

Anywhere a name appears, you can replace it by its definition, and anywhere an expression appears, you can replace it by its value, without changing what the program means.

This property has a name: referential transparency. It is what lets you reason about each piece of a functional program separately, the way you simplify one part of an algebraic equation without worrying about the rest.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
8.6 When substitution breaks
Now consider a function that changes a mutable variable:
let mutable counter = 0
let nextId () =
    counter <- counter + 1
    counter

let x1 = nextId () + nextId ()   // 1 + 2 = 3
let x2 = 2 * nextId ()           // 2 * 3 = 6
In mathematics, f(x) + f(x) = 2\,f(x) holds for every function f and every x. Here, with x being (), nextId () + nextId () is 3, but 2 * nextId () is 6. The expression nextId () does not have one fixed value: it depends on when it is evaluated, and evaluating it changes the world for everyone else. You can no longer replace nextId () by “its value”, because it has none. To understand this code, you are back to replaying steps in order.
Mutation is not the only culprit. Any side effect breaks substitution in the same way:

printfn "Hi" has the value (), but replacing it by () changes the program: the output disappears.
Reading the clock gives a different value each time. After the lines below, t1 and t2 may differ, even though they come from the same expression:
let t1 = System.DateTime.Now
let t2 = System.DateTime.Now     // same expression, possibly a different value
The same holds for reading input, files, or the network, and for random numbers.

This is the real reason functional programmers avoid mutation and keep other side effects at the edges of a program. It isn’t a matter of style. Wherever there are side effects, the simple reasoning of this section stops working, and you are back to replaying steps in order.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
section: 9.1 Why it matters: sharing is safe
text:
9.1 Why it matters: sharing is safe
Arrays are one of the few mutable things in F#. Look at what happens when two names refer to the same array:
let scores = [| 70; 80; 90 |]   // an array: mutable
let backup = scores             // NOT a copy!
scores[0] <- 0
let surprise = backup[0]        // 0: backup changed too
backup was supposed to be a safety copy, but let backup = scores only gives the same array a second name. Changing it through one name changes it for the other. This kind of bug, called aliasing, is common in every imperative language, and gets much worse in large programs and in programs that run several things at once (Week 12).
With immutable values, aliasing is harmless. If nobody can change a value, it does not matter how many names refer to it. You can pass it to any function, store it anywhere, share it between threads, and it stays what it was.

title: Week 1 · Programs as Expressions
text:
9.2 Mutation is available, but explicit
F# does allow mutable variables, with let mutable and the assignment operator <-, as in the counter example. It is a tool for special situations, such as a tight loop where performance matters, or code that talks to libraries written in an imperative style. In this course, use it only when you can say why.






Warning= is not assignment



In F#, = compares. <- assigns.
> let mutable x = 1;;
val mutable x: int = 1

> x = 2;;
val it: bool = false
x = 2 does not change x; it asks “is x equal to 2?” and answers false. If you meant to assign, write x <- 2.

title: Week 2 · Drills
text:
Recursion becomes easy only through repetition, so this sheet is long on purpose. Each section has three tiers:

Core: everyone does these. We do some of them in class.
Practice: more of the same shape. Do these until the recipe feels automatic.
Stretch: harder variations, for when the core feels easy.

Work on paper first, then check in FSI. For every function you write, go through the four steps of the recipe: type, base case, recursive case, check.
Unless a question says otherwise, use these definitions from the notes:
let rec sumTo n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | n -> n + sumTo (n - 1)

let rec power x n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 1.0
    | n -> x * power x (n - 1)

let rec repeat s n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> ""
    | n -> s + repeat s (n - 1)

let rec binary n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> "0"
    | 1 -> "1"
    | n -> binary (n / 2) + string (n % 2)

let rec digitSum n =
    match n with
    | n when n < 10 -> n
    | n -> n % 10 + digitSum (n / 10)

let rec gcd a b =
    match b with
    | 0 -> a
    | b -> gcd b (a % b)

let rec fib n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | 1 -> 1
    | n -> fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2)

let add x y = x + y
let twice f x = f (f x)

A. Trace by hand
Write the evaluation step by step until you reach a value. For Core, write a full trace, numbering each step with the rule you used (including rule 7 for match), for at least A1. For the others, the equation style (sumTo 3 = 3 + sumTo 2 = …) is enough.
Core

sumTo 4 (full trace)
power 3.0 2
binary 13
gcd 84 36. How many calls to gcd happen in total?

Practice

repeat "-" 3
digitSum 9075

Stretch

Draw all the calls made by fib 5 as a tree, with fib 5 at the top and each call’s children below it. How many calls are there in total? How many times is fib 3 computed? Why does this explain the slowness of fib 40?







TipAnswers





1.   sumTo 4
   ⇝ match 4 with | 0 -> 0 | n -> n + sumTo (n - 1)     (3)
   ⇝ 4 + sumTo (4 - 1)                                  (7) 4 isn't 0; n ↦ 4
   ⇝ 4 + sumTo 3                                        (4)
   ⇝ 4 + (3 + sumTo 2)                                  (3),(7),(4)
   ⇝ 4 + (3 + (2 + sumTo 1))                            (3),(7),(4)
   ⇝ 4 + (3 + (2 + (1 + sumTo 0)))                      (3),(7),(4)
   ⇝ 4 + (3 + (2 + (1 + 0)))                            (3),(7) 0 fits
   ⇝ 4 + (3 + (2 + 1))  ⇝  4 + (3 + 3)  ⇝  4 + 6  ⇝  10  (4)

2.   power 3.0 2 = 3.0 * power 3.0 1
                 = 3.0 * (3.0 * power 3.0 0)
                 = 3.0 * (3.0 * 1.0)
                 = 9.0

3.   binary 13 = binary 6 + "1"                 13 = 2 × 6 + 1
               = (binary 3 + "0") + "1"         6 = 2 × 3 + 0
               = ((binary 1 + "1") + "0") + "1" 3 = 2 × 1 + 1
               = "1" + "1" + "0" + "1"
               = "1101"

4.   gcd 84 36 = gcd 36 12       84 % 36 = 12
               = gcd 12 0        36 % 12 = 0
               = 12              three calls in total

5.   repeat "-" 3 = "-" + ("-" + ("-" + "")) = "---"

6.   digitSum 9075 = 5 + digitSum 907
                   = 5 + (7 + digitSum 90)
                   = 5 + (7 + (0 + digitSum 9))
                   = 5 + (7 + (0 + 9))
                   = 21

The tree has 15 calls. fib 3 is computed twice, fib 2 three times, fib 1 five times. Every call to fib n (for n ≥ 2) makes two more calls, and the two subtrees overlap almost completely, so the number of calls grows about as fast as the Fibonacci numbers themselves: roughly ×1.6 for each step. fib 40 makes over 300 million calls.






B. From equations to F
Each function is given as equations. Write it in F# with match, and give its type.
Core

The sum of the squares 0^2 + 1^2 + \cdots + n^2:  \mathit{sq}(0) = 0 \qquad \mathit{sq}(n) = n^2 + \mathit{sq}(n-1)  sumOfSquares 3 should be 14.
A rocket countdown: countdown 3 should be "3 2 1 liftoff".  \mathit{cd}(0) = \text{"liftoff"} \qquad \mathit{cd}(n) = n \text{ followed by a space and } \mathit{cd}(n-1) 
Multiplication by repeated addition (no * allowed):  a \cdot 0 = 0 \qquad a \cdot b = a + a \cdot (b - 1) 

Practice

numDigits: the number of decimal digits of a natural number. numDigits 9075 = 4, numDigits 7 = 1. Hint: look at digitSum, and write the equations first.
Tower of Hanoi. Moving a stack of n discs takes h(n) moves, where  h(0) = 0 \qquad h(n) = 2\,h(n-1) + 1  Write hanoi, and compute hanoi 10. Can you guess a formula for hanoi n?

Stretch

Generalise binary to any base from 2 to 10: toBase 8 64 = "100", toBase 10 1234 = "1234". Which order should the parameters be in, so that let octal = toBase 8 works?
The Ackermann function is a famous example of a function that grows extremely fast: 
A(0, n) = n + 1 \qquad A(m, 0) = A(m - 1, 1) \qquad A(m, n) = A(m - 1,\ A(m, n - 1))
 Write ack m n. You will need a match inside a match. Check that ack 2 3 = 9 and ack 3 3 = 61. Don’t try ack 4 2: the answer has 19,729 digits.







TipAnswers





let rec sumOfSquares n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | n -> n * n + sumOfSquares (n - 1)

let rec countdown n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> "liftoff"
    | n -> string n + " " + countdown (n - 1)

let rec mul a b =
    match b with
    | 0 -> 0
    | b -> a + mul a (b - 1)
Types: sumOfSquares: int -> int, countdown: int -> string, mul: int -> int -> int.
let rec numDigits n =
    match n with
    | n when n < 10 -> 1
    | n -> 1 + numDigits (n / 10)

let rec hanoi n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | n -> 2 * hanoi (n - 1) + 1
hanoi 10 = 1023. The formula is h(n) = 2^n - 1 (you can prove it by induction, as in the notes).
let digitChar d = string d        // digits 0-9 only, enough for bases up to 10

let rec toBase b n =
    match n with
    | n when n < b -> digitChar n
    | n -> toBase b (n / b) + digitChar (n % b)

let octal = toBase 8

let rec ack m n =
    match m with
    | 0 -> n + 1
    | m ->
        match n with
        | 0 -> ack (m - 1) 1
        | n -> ack (m - 1) (ack m (n - 1))
The base must come first, so that partial application fixes it: toBase 8 is a function waiting for the number. Notice how toBase is binary with 2 replaced by b, and how the base case is a range (n < b) instead of two constants.





C. if and match
Core

Rewrite with match and a guard:
let absolute n = if n < 0 then -n else n
Rewrite Week 1’s shippingFee using match with guards instead of if/elif:
let shippingFee weight =
    if weight <= 1 then 40
    elif weight <= 5 then 40 + (weight - 1) * 15
    else 100 + (weight - 5) * 10

Practice

Now the other direction. Rewrite isWeekend from the notes without match and without if, as a single boolean expression.

Stretch

For each of the three functions above, which version do you find clearer, and why? Is there a general rule?







TipAnswers





let absolute n =
    match n with
    | n when n < 0 -> -n
    | n -> n

let shippingFee weight =
    match weight with
    | w when w <= 1 -> 40
    | w when w <= 5 -> 40 + (w - 1) * 15
    | w -> 100 + (w - 5) * 10

let isWeekendIf day = day = "Saturday" || day = "Sunday"

There is no single right answer. A reasonable rule: when the cases are ranges of one value (as in shippingFee), match with guards and if/elif are about equally clear. When the cases are specific values, match is clearer. When the answer is itself a yes/no, a boolean expression is often simplest. From Week 4 on, match wins almost every time, because it can take apart structured values.






D. Find the bug
Each function is wrong. Say what happens when you use it (error, warning, wrong answer, or crash), and fix it.
Core

let rec sumTo n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 0
    | n -> n + sumTo n
let fact n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> 1
    | n -> n * fact (n - 1)
let rec fact n =
    match n with
    | n -> n * fact (n - 1)
    | 0 -> 1
let rec repeat s n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> s
    | n -> s + repeat s (n - 1)

Practice

What does binary 6 give with this version? Why?
let rec binary n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> "0"
    | n -> binary (n / 2) + string (n % 2)
This works for some inputs and crashes on others. Which ones?
let rec countdown n =
    match n with
    | 0 -> "liftoff"
    | n -> string n + " " + countdown (n - 2)

Stretch

fact 13 returns 1932053504. Is that correct? What happened, and how do you fix it?







TipAnswers






The recursive call sumTo n doesn’t make the input smaller, so it never reaches 0: stack overflow for any input except 0. Fix: sumTo (n - 1).
Missing rec: error FS0039, The value or constructor 'fact' is not defined.
The first rule catches everything, so the base case is never used: warning FS0026, This rule will never be matched, and then a stack overflow at run time. Fix: put | 0 -> 1 first.
Wrong base case: repeating s zero times should give "", not s. Now repeat "ab" 2 gives "ababab", one copy too many. An off-by-one error with no warning at all. The check step (trace a small input!) catches it.
"0110", with a leading zero. binary 1 = binary 0 + "1" = "01", and that extra "0" appears at the front of every result. The fix is the second base case | 1 -> "1".
It subtracts 2, so it only reaches 0 from even numbers. countdown 4 = "4 2 liftoff" works, but countdown 3 goes 3, 1, -1, -3, …: stack overflow. The measure (the notes’ “going further” box) doesn’t reach the base case.
Not correct: 13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800, which is bigger than the largest int (about 2.1 billion). int arithmetic wraps around silently. Fix: use int64 (factBig 13L in the notes) or bigint.






E. Read the type
Write the type FSI will report. Then check in FSI.
Core

let rec f n = match n with 0 -> "" | n -> "*" + f (n - 1)
let g x y = x * y + 0.5
